qs.q: A child being treated for acute chickenpox is given salicylates to control fever and subsequently develops fulminant encephalitis and severe hepatic dysfunction. What syndrome is strongly associated with this medication use during VZV infection?
qs.e: Fulminant encephalitis during chickenpox can be part of Reye's syndrome if salicylates are administered to children. Post-herpetic neuralgia is a complication of shingles involving chronic pain rather than salicylate-induced liver and brain dysfunction.
qs.s: Herpesviruses: HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV, Symptoms, Diagnosis, Tx: MCQs

qs.q: A 10-year-old child is exposed to chickenpox. The child is healthy and not immunocompromised. Which of the following is the most appropriate preventive measure if given within the recommended window?
o: Administration of live attenuated varicella vaccine
qs.e: The live attenuated varicella vaccine is used for active prevention in healthy children aged 1-12 years. VZIG is for passive immunity in immunocompromised or high-risk cases, and acyclovir is for treatment.
qs.s: Herpesviruses: HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV, Symptoms, Diagnosis, Tx: MCQs

qs.q: Why is the administration of aspirin strictly contraindicated in children suffering from chickenpox (varicella)?
qs.e: Salicylate use during primary varicella infection can trigger fulminant encephalitis known as Reye's syndrome, making aspirin use dangerous in children with chickenpox. Antivirals and antibiotics do not mediate this specific fatal syndrome.
qs.s: Herpesviridae: HSV-1, HSV-2 Pathogenesis & Clinical Diseases: MCQs

qs.q: Which of the following describes the characteristic progression and distribution of the rash in uncomplicated varicella (chickenpox)?
o: Painless mucosal ulcers on the cervix
Simultaneous crops starting on the trunk
Rapidly coalescing purpuric macules on palms
Strictly unilateral lesions on a single dermatome
qs.e: Chickenpox features cropping, where lesions are in different stages simultaneously (macules, papules, vesicles, crusts), starting on the trunk and spreading to the face and limbs. Unilateral vesicular lesions restricted to a single dermatome describe herpes zoster, not primary varicella.
qs.s: Herpesviridae: HSV-1, HSV-2 Pathogenesis & Clinical Diseases: MCQs

qs.q: A patient presents with a disseminated vesicular rash where all skin lesions appear at the exact same developmental stage simultaneously, unlike the successive crops seen in chickenpox. This characteristic synchronous rash is a hallmark of infection with which agent?
qs.e: Smallpox lesions are characteristically synchronous, appearing all at the same stage at the same time, unlike the asynchronous crops of varicella. Measles and rubella present with maculopapular rashes rather than vesicular synchronous ones.
qs.s: Medical Virology Semester 3 Crash Revision: MCQs

qs.q: What is the major site of latency for the Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV) following primary chickenpox infection?
qs.e: Varicella-Zoster Virus establishes latency in sensory ganglia, similar to HSV-1 and HSV-2. B lymphocytes serve as the major site of latency for Epstein-Barr virus instead.
qs.s: Mycology Revision: Fungal Infections, Histoplasmosis & Cryptococcosis: MCQs

qs.q: What is the drug of choice for treating complicated chickenpox, VZV in immunocompromised patients, and neonatal varicella?
qs.e: Acyclovir is the drug of choice for VZV and inhibits viral DNA polymerase, though it does not affect latency. Ganciclovir is used for CMV infections.
qs.s: Herpesviridae: HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, Treatment: MCQs

qs.q: An immunocompromised child who has been exposed to chickenpox is given passive prophylaxis. What specific biological product is administered?
qs.e: VZIG (Varicella-Zoster Immunoglobulin) is given for passive prevention to exposed immunocompromised children and mothers infected near term. The vaccine is for active immunization in healthy children.
qs.s: Herpesviridae: HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, Treatment: MCQs

es.q: A pregnant woman in her first trimester is diagnosed with primary varicella. 1. What is the potential risk to the fetus if this infection occurs early in pregnancy? 2. Describe the characteristic appearance of the rash in chickenpox (varicella) in a child. 3. Name a severe neurological complication
es.m: 1. The fetus is at risk of Congenital Varicella Syndrome, which can manifest as skin lesions, limb hypoplasia, chorioretinitis, and CNS defects. 2. The rash progresses from macules to papules to vesicles to crusts, typically starting on the trunk and spreading to the face and limbs. A characteristic feature is "cropping," where lesions at different stages are present simultaneously. 3. Fulminant encephalitis, which can be part of Reye's syndrome if salicylates are given.
es.s: Herpesviridae: HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, Treatment — Practice Q
